question.text: The line shown above passes through the points $(0,3)$ and $(-2,-1).$ What is the equation of the line?
question.explanation:
We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form $y=mx+b.$ So we need to work out the slope $m$ and the $y$-intercept $b.$

From the graph, we see that the line intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,3).$ So, the $y$-intercept is $b=3.$

We can calculate the slope of the line by choosing two points on the line and applying the slope formula. The line passes through the points $(0,3)$ and $(-2,-1),$ so we calculate its slope as follows: \begin{align*} m &= \dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{-1-3}{-2-0} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{-4}{-2} \\[5pt] &= 2 \end{align*}

Substituting the slope $m=2$ and the $y$-intercept $b=3$ into the slope-intercept form $y=mx+b,$ we obtain the equation of the line:

\[ y=2x+3 \]

topic.name: Equations of Lines in Slope-Intercept Form

question.explanation:
We convert the absolute value inequality into a compound inequality to remove the absolute value.

The inequality specifies every number $12z+7$ whose distance from zero is greater than or equal to $5.$ This corresponds to the following compound inequality:

\begin{align} 12z+7 &\leq -5 & \text{or} & & 12z+7 &\geq 5 \end{align}

Now, we can solve each inequality using the usual methods.

\begin{align*} 12z+7 &\leq -5 &&& 12z+7 &\geq 5 \\[5pt] 12z &\leq -12 &&& 12z &\geq -2 \\[5pt] z &\leq -1 &&& z &\geq -\dfrac 16 \end{align*}

Therefore, the final solution is

\begin{align} z &\leq \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-1} & \text{or} & & z &\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\geq}\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\dfrac 16}. \end{align}

question.text: What is the solution to the following system of inequalities? \[ \begin{cases} p-2 > 3 \\[5pt] 1-2p \leq -7 \end{cases} \]
question.explanation:
To solve the system, we need to find the values of $p$ that satisfy both $p-2 > 3$ and $1-2p \leq -7$ simultaneously.

  • First, we solve $p-2 > 3 \,\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} p-2 &> 3 \\[5pt] p-2+2 &> 3+2 \\[5pt] p & > 5 \end{align*}

\[ \]

  • Then, we solve $1-2p \leq -7 \,\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} 1-2p &\leq -7 \\[5pt] 1-2p-1 &\leq -7-1 \\[5pt] -2p &\leq -8 \\[5pt] (-1)\cdot(-2p) &\geq (-1)\cdot(-8) \\[5pt] 2p &\geq 8\\[5pt] \dfrac{2p}{2} &\geq \dfrac{8}{2} \\[5pt] p &\geq 4 \end{align*}

To find the values of $p$ that satisfy both inequalities, we find where the two solutions overlap:

\[\]

Thus, the final solution is $p\in (5,\infty).$

question.text: What is $0.9 \, \textrm{g}$ expressed in $\textrm{mg}?$ Write your answer as a whole number.
question.explanation:
We start by recalling the conversion table for mass units.

Name Symbol Conversion
Kilogram $\textrm{kg}$ $1\,\textrm{kg} = 1\,000\,\textrm{g} $
Gram $\textrm{g}$ Base Unit
Milligram $\textrm{mg}$ $1\,000\,\textrm{mg} = 1\,\textrm{g}$
\[ \]

There are $1\,000\,\textrm {mg}$ per $\textrm{g},$ which we can write as follows: \[ \dfrac{1000\,\textrm{mg}}{\textrm{g}} \]

This is our conversion factor.

Now, multiplying $0.9 \,\textrm{g} $ by our conversion factor, we get \begin{align*} \require{cancel} 0.9 \,\textrm{g} &= 0.9 \,\textrm{g} \cdot \dfrac{1\,000\,\textrm{mg}}{\textrm{g}} \\[5pt] &= 0.9 \,\cancel{\textrm{g}} \cdot \dfrac{1\,000\,\textrm{mg}}{\cancel{\textrm{g}}} \\[5pt] &= 0.9 \cdot 1\,000\,\textrm{mg} \\[5pt] & = 900 \,\textrm{mg}. \end{align*}

Therefore, $0.9 \,\textrm{g}$ is equivalent to $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{900} \,\text{mg}.$

topic.name: Unit Conversions Using Base Units of Mass

question.text: Given that the triangle $\triangle{ABC}$ shown above is isosceles, the measure of $\overline{AC}$ must be equal to
question.explanation:
Since $\triangle{ABC}$ is an isosceles triangle with base $\overline{AB}$, we have that $\overline{AC} \cong \overline{CB}.$ Hence,

\begin{align*} AC &= CB\\[5pt] 3x-9 &=2x-1\\[5pt] x &= 8. \end{align*}

Substituting this value into the expression for the measure of $\overline{AC}$ gives

\begin{align*} AC &= 3x-9 \\[3pt] &= 3(8) -9 \\[3pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{15}. \end{align*}

example.title: Solving for a Variable Given Unknown Lengths in an Isosceles Triangle

question.text: In the diagram shown above, $B$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AD}.$ Find $BC$ if $AD = 29 \, \text{cm}$ and $CD= 6.5 \, \text{cm}.$
question.explanation:
Since $B$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AD}$, we have:

\begin{align} BD & = \dfrac{1}{2} AD \\[3pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 29 \\[3pt] & = 14.5 \, \text{cm} \end{align}

Now, by the segment addition postulate, we obtain:

\begin{align} BD & = BC + CD \\[3pt] 14.5 & = BC + 6.5 \\[3pt] 14.5-6.5 & = BC \\[3pt] BC & = 8 \, \text{cm} \end{align}

example.title: Calculating the Value of an Unknown Quantity Using Collinearity and Midpoints

question.text: What is the area of the right triangle $ABC$ shown above?
question.explanation:
Since $m\angle{A}=m\angle{C}=45^\circ$ and $AB=BC,$ we have an isosceles right triangle.

Therefore, the area of the triangle is

\begin{align*} \mathcal{A} & = \dfrac{1}{2} AB \cdot BC\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 8^2\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 64\\[5pt] & = 32. \end{align*}
